column1: 359|A haloalkane has halogen bonded to an aliphatic sp³ carbon (e.g. CH₃CH₂Cl). A haloarene has halogen directly bonded to an aromatic-ring carbon (e.g. chlorobenzene).
360|2-Bromobutane.
361|Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻.
362|Bond strength decreases C–F>C–Cl>C–Br>C–I as bond length increases. For substitution, easier C–X cleavage generally gives RI>RBr>RCl≫RF, although mechanism and substrate also matter.
363|Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group (often halide) on carbon with a nucleophile: R–X+Nu⁻→R–Nu+X⁻.

364|SN1 is two-step, through a carbocation; rate=k[RX], often favoured by tertiary substrate/polar protic solvent and gives racemisation tendency. SN2 is concerted backside attack; rate=k[RX][Nu⁻], favoured by less hindered substrate/strong nucleophile and gives inversion.

365|Tertiary substrates form relatively stable carbocations and are sterically hindered to backside attack, favouring SN1. Primary substrates form unstable carbocations but allow backside approach, favouring SN2; solvent/nucleophile can alter the outcome.
366|Racemisation is loss of optical purity as an initially optically active substrate forms a mixture of enantiomers, often through attack on both faces of a planar carbocation.
367|SN2 proceeds by backside attack as the C–Nu bond forms and C–X breaks, causing inversion of configuration at the reacting stereogenic centre (Walden inversion).
368|Optical activity is the ability of a chiral substance to rotate the plane of plane-polarised light; enantiomers rotate it equally in opposite directions.
369|SN1 forms a roughly planar carbocation, which can be attacked from either face, producing both configurations. Ion-pair effects often make racemisation incomplete rather than exactly 50:50.
370|SN1 reactivity generally 3°>2°>1° because increasing alkyl substitution stabilises the rate-determining carbocation.

371|Major product is butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, by nucleophilic substitution with aqueous OH⁻ replacing Br⁻; secondary-substrate elimination can be a minor competing pathway depending on conditions.
372|Dehydrohalogenation is elimination of HX from adjacent (α and β) carbons of a haloalkane to form an alkene, commonly with alcoholic base and heat.
373|Aqueous KOH favours nucleophilic substitution to an alcohol. Alcoholic KOH with heat favours β-elimination to an alkene; substrate and conditions can allow competing pathways.
374|Aryl C–X has partial double-bond character from resonance, the bonded carbon is sp², and backside attack/phenyl-cation formation is difficult; haloarenes therefore resist ordinary SN reactions.

375|A chlorine lone pair overlaps with the benzene π system. Resonance contributors place π bonding between C and Cl, giving the aryl C–Cl bond partial double-bond character and shortening/strengthening it.

376|Cl donates a lone pair by resonance, increasing electron density mainly at ortho and para positions and stabilising the corresponding arenium intermediates; these positions are therefore directed despite deactivation.
377|The strong −I effect withdraws electron density and deactivates the ring. Lone-pair resonance donation stabilises ortho/para substitution intermediates, so halogens remain ortho/para directors.
378|Nitration gives ortho- and para-nitrochlorobenzene, with the para isomer generally major because it is less sterically crowded.
379|Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether: 2R–X+2Na→R–R+2NaX.
380|Fittig reaction couples aryl halides with sodium in dry ether: 2Ar–X+2Na→Ar–Ar+2NaX.
381|Wurtz–Fittig reaction couples an aryl and an alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether: Ar–X+R–X+2Na→Ar–R+2NaX.
382|Principal Wurtz–Fittig product is toluene: C₆H₅Br+CH₃Br+2Na→C₆H₅CH₃+2NaBr. Homocoupling side-products (biphenyl and ethane) may also form.
383|Heat the haloalkane with aqueous NaOH or KOH to replace X by OH: R–X+OH⁻→R–OH+X⁻.
384|Convert ethanol to bromoethane with HBr (often generated from NaBr/KBr and concentrated H₂SO₄) or use PBr₃: CH₃CH₂OH→CH₃CH₂Br.
385|An allylic halide has X on an sp³ carbon adjacent to C=C; a vinylic halide has X directly attached to an alkene (sp²) carbon.
386|Vinyl C–Cl has partial double-bond character through conjugation, is shorter/stronger at an sp² carbon and resists backside attack; ethyl chloride has an ordinary sp³ C–Cl bond.

387|Dichloromethane is used as an industrial solvent and in paint strippers. Emissions contribute to stratospheric ozone depletion despite its relatively short atmospheric lifetime (Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme evaluation, 2021).
388|Chloroform has been used as a solvent and historically as an anaesthetic. It can damage liver/kidneys and depress the central nervous system; it is unsafe for unsupervised exposure.
389|CCl₄ is toxic and persistent, and chlorine radicals released in the stratosphere catalytically deplete ozone; its production/use has been heavily restricted.
390|Iodoform is triiodomethane, CHI₃, a yellow crystalline solid historically used as an antiseptic/dressing because it releases iodine-containing species.

391|Freons are chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) refrigerants/propellants. Stable CFCs reach the stratosphere and release chlorine radicals that deplete ozone; many were phased out under the Montreal Protocol.
392|DDT is persistent, fat-soluble and bioaccumulates/biomagnifies, harming wildlife (notably birds) and potentially exposing people through food chains.

393|DDT is notably persistent and bioaccumulative. Many newer pesticides are designed to degrade faster, but persistence and bioaccumulation vary by compound; some modern pesticides remain hazardous, so a blanket claim that all are safer is not justified.
394|For the same alkyl group, molar mass and polarizability generally rise F→Cl→Br→I, strengthening dispersion forces; boiling points usually rise in that order (with structural exceptions).
395|Branching makes isomers more compact, reducing intermolecular contact surface and London dispersion forces; less energy is required to separate molecules, so boiling point generally falls.
396|Haloalkanes cannot hydrogen-bond effectively with water, and their hydrophobic alkyl group makes hydration energetically unfavourable; only slight amounts dissolve.

397|Many organic solvents have compatible polarizability and dispersion interactions with haloalkanes, so solute–solvent attractions can offset disruption of solvent–solvent interactions despite C–X bond polarity.
398|A Grignard reagent is an organomagnesium halide, RMgX, containing a strongly polar C–Mg bond and behaving as a powerful nucleophilic/basic carbon reagent.
399|Water protonates the carbon end and destroys the reagent: RMgX+H₂O→RH+Mg(OH)X. Dry ether coordinates/stabilises Mg and must also be anhydrous.
400|CH₃CH₂Br+Mg→CH₃CH₂MgBr in dry ether.
401|RMgX+CO₂→RCO₂MgX; acidic hydrolysis gives RCOOH. The carboxylic acid has one more carbon than R.

402|Use sodium fusion (Lassaigne’s test) to convert halogen to NaX in the extract; acidify with dilute HNO₃, then add AgNO₃. AgCl is white, AgBr pale yellow and AgI yellow; confirmatory solubility tests can distinguish them.

403|Covalently bound halogen may not release X⁻ simply on contact with aqueous AgNO₃, especially for aryl/vinyl halides. The test depends on hydrolysis/ionisation and solubility, so sample preparation and suitable reaction conditions are needed.
404|A nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electrophilic atom (often carbon) to form a bond. A base accepts a proton; many species can do both, but the attacked site differs.

405|Polar protic solvents stabilise ions/carbocations and solvate anionic nucleophiles, often favouring SN1 and slowing SN2. Polar aprotic solvents solvate cations but leave nucleophiles reactive, often accelerating SN2.
406|A leaving group departs from carbon with the bonding electron pair, enabling substitution. Stable, weakly basic anions generally leave more readily.
407|Typical ability: I⁻>Br⁻>Cl⁻≫F⁻. Larger, more polarizable anions are more stable and weaker bases, and the C–I bond is weakest; the exact rate still depends on substrate and mechanism.
408|2-Chlorobutane.
409|Propene is the major product: CH₃CHBrCH₃+KOH(alc)→CH₃CH=CH₂+KBr+H₂O. Alcoholic base and heat favour concerted E2 β-elimination.
410|Tert-butyl chloride forms a relatively stable tertiary carbocation; a polar protic solvent stabilises the developing ions, accelerating the SN1 ionisation step.

411|SN1 has two transition states separated by a carbocation intermediate; the first, ionisation barrier is often rate-determining. SN2 has one concerted transition state and one barrier, with simultaneous C–Nu formation and C–X cleavage.
412|Inversion of configuration is reversal of the spatial arrangement at a stereogenic carbon, as in backside SN2 attack (Walden inversion).
413|Likely SN2: the strong nucleophile attacks from the backside in polar aprotic solvent, producing inversion at the reacting chiral centre, provided steric hindrance does not prevent SN2.

414|Chlorobenzene’s aryl C–Cl bond has resonance partial double-bond character and is attached to an sp² carbon; ordinary backside substitution is difficult, so hydrolysis requires much harsher conditions than for alkyl chlorides.

415|Ortho/para electron-withdrawing groups stabilise the negatively charged Meisenheimer addition intermediate by resonance delocalisation, lowering the barrier for nucleophilic aromatic substitution.
416|Bromoethane hydrolyses to ethanol: CH₃CH₂Br+OH⁻→CH₃CH₂OH+Br⁻.
417|Add HBr to propene in the presence of peroxide (ROOR), usually with heat/light: radical anti-Markovnikov addition gives CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (1-bromopropane).
418|Dry ether solvates/stabilises the sodium and organometallic intermediates and provides an inert medium; moisture would consume sodium or protonate reactive species.
419|Each haloalkane can couple with either partner, producing both cross-coupled and homocoupled products. The mixture is difficult to avoid unless the reactants are chosen carefully.
420|UV light breaks C–Cl bonds in stratospheric CFCs, releasing chlorine radicals. These radicals catalytically convert ozone to oxygen and are regenerated.
421|Cl·+O₃→ClO·+O₂; then ClO·+O·→Cl·+O₂. Chlorine radical is regenerated, so the net reaction is O₃+O→2O₂ and one radical can destroy many ozone molecules.
422|A geminal dihalide has both halogen atoms on the same carbon; a vicinal dihalide has them on adjacent carbons.

423|Allyl chloride is highly reactive because its transition state/carbocation is resonance-stabilised; ethyl chloride has ordinary primary-halide reactivity; vinyl chloride is much less reactive because its sp² C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character. Typical order: allyl chloride>ethyl chloride≫vinyl chloride.
424|Halogens are much heavier and more polarizable than hydrogen, so replacing H with one or more halogens raises molar mass and often density relative to the corresponding hydrocarbon.

425|A new stereogenic centre forms if substitution gives a carbon attached to four different groups. Assign R/S by CIP priorities (atomic number, then successive ties); determine whether the mechanism gives inversion, racemisation or another stereochemical outcome separately.
426|Propanenitrile (ethyl cyanide), CH₃CH₂C≡N; KCN attacks through carbon, adding one carbon to the chain.
427|KCN is ionic and supplies free CN⁻, which attacks through carbon to give propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN. Covalent AgCN favours nitrogen-end attack, giving ethyl isocyanide, CH₃CH₂NC.
428|SN2 is a single concerted collision of haloalkane and nucleophile, so its rate law is rate=k[RX][Nu⁻]; increasing either reactant concentration increases the frequency of productive encounters.
